revision_history.description: First issue. Authored because no artefact of type implementation existed and the as_is corpus anchors the UART driver through three source anchors (FB2-SRC-COD-000067, -000068, -000069) plus the flow-control constant header anchor FB2-SRC-COD-000070, with no design artefact covering it.

implements.relationship: No design artefact in the as_is profile describes the UART driver, so there is no design for this element to implement and no implements link is asserted. What the module does, read from the pinned source: UART_Initialize (uart.c:144-164) configures the SCI peripheral and registers the receive interrupt. UART_RxInterrupt (244-263) distinguishes the two flow-control characters from ordinary data - if the byte just received equals UART_XOFF or UART_XON it updates the software sending state, otherwise, and only once the task queues exist, it posts the byte onto ftsk_uartRxQueue and notifies the UART task with a yield-if-needed request. UART_HandleFlowControl (223-242) is the transmitter's half: it takes the transmit semaphore, and when the number of stored receive-queue messages reaches UART_UPPER_CUTOFF_MESSAGE_COUNT it sends the XOFF character and marks the receiving side as paused, and when the count falls to UART_LOWER_CUTOFF_MESSAGE_COUNT it sends XON and resumes - so the flow control is a software, queue-depth-driven XON/XOFF scheme rather than a hardware one. UART_Read (196-221) pulls bytes out of that queue for the task. So the driver provides an interrupt-driven queued byte stream with in-band software flow control.

behaviours.description: Configures the SCI peripheral and registers the receive interrupt that feeds the driver.
Receive interrupt: treats XON and XOFF as flow-control state changes and every other byte as data to enqueue and to notify the task for.
Drives software flow control from the receive queue's depth, sending XOFF at the upper cutoff and XON at the lower cutoff, under the transmit semaphore.
Drains received bytes from the queue into a caller buffer, so the task layer never reads the peripheral register directly.

concurrency_and_isr_context.shared_state: ftsk_uartRxQueue, which the interrupt fills through OS_SendToBackOfQueueFromIsr and UART_Read drains in task context, plus the module-scope flags uart_softwareFlowControlReceiving and uart_softwareFlowControlSending, which the interrupt sets and UART_HandleFlowControl reads.
The same receive queue, and uart_txSemaphore, which UART_HandleFlowControl takes and gives around each flow-control character it sends.

guard.statement: This record says where the UART driver code is and what it does. It implements no design artefact and realises no requirement in this profile, and both gaps are declared. It is not evidence that any requirement is met: in particular nothing here establishes that the service link is authenticated or that any byte received on it is authorised, which is what the security requirements would have to demand of it. It confers no production authority, no verification credit and no human approval.
